section.title: Trigonometric substitution
section.p: Trigonometric integrals used identities after trigonometric functions were already present. Trigonometric substitution uses those identities earlier. It creates trigonometric functions on purpose.

A trigonometric substitution chooses x so that the square root becomes a simpler trigonometric expression. The square root does not vanish by magic. It vanishes because a right triangle or a circle was hidden inside it.

exercise.title: Why does a square root such as \sqrt{a^2-x^2} hide a triangle?

statement.p: The expression \sqrt{9-x^2} is the upper half of a circle. In your own words, why does choosing x=3\sin\theta make the square root become 3\cos\theta, and why is that not magic but a Pythagorean identity?

hint.p: The substitution is chosen so that a^2-x^2 becomes a perfect square. A point on the circle of radius a already has coordinates that satisfy that identity.

statement.p: The three patterns \sqrt{a^2-x^2}, \sqrt{a^2+x^2}, and \sqrt{x^2-a^2} match sine, tangent, and secant substitutions. The condition x>2 is not a small detail. The substitution x=2\sec\theta with 0\le\theta<\pi/2 covers x\ge2. On another interval, such as x<-2, we would choose a different range or adjust the substitution. Antiderivatives are always local to an interval where the integrand is defined.

subsection.title: Returning to the original variable
subsection.p: An indefinite integral should end in the original variable unless the new variable has been clearly defined.
There are two common ways to return.

row.cell: Uses the substitution to draw a triangle and read \sin\theta, \cos\theta, \tan\theta, or \sec\theta.

subsection.p: In many examples, both methods are needed. The angle \theta itself becomes an inverse trigonometric function. Other expressions, such as \sin2\theta or \tan\theta, are easiest to recover from the triangle.

paragraphs.title: Definite integrals: change the limits
paragraphs.p: For definite integrals, there is often no need to return to x. We can change the limits instead.
No x-triangle is needed at the end because the whole calculation stayed in the new variable after the limits changed.

note.title: A common mistake
note.p: Do not mix variables in a definite integral. After substituting x=2\sin\theta, either change the limits to \theta-limits or return the antiderivative to x before evaluating.

exercise.title: Why can a definite trigonometric substitution skip returning to x?

statement.p: For a definite integral, we can change the limits to \theta-values and never go back. In your own words, why are the limits part of the substitution, and when would you still need a triangle to return to the original variable?

hint.p: An indefinite answer must be written in x. A definite integral only needs the accumulated amount between the new endpoints.

exercise.title: Why does the range of \theta matter?

statement.p: After substitution, a square root becomes something like a|\cos\theta|. In your own words, why do we choose a range of \theta so that the square root is nonnegative without an absolute value, and why can the same-looking formula fail on a different interval of x?

hint.p: A triangle carries sign information. The substitution x=a\sec\theta with 0\le\theta<\pi/2 covers x\ge a, not the separate piece x\le -a.

The hyperbolic substitution gives the logarithmic answer more directly. It is not a new kind of calculus. It is another choice of variable matched to the shape of the square root.

Trigonometric substitution handles square roots by changing the geometry of the variable. The next family of integrals has no square roots at all. It is algebraic: one polynomial divided by another. There the right move is not to create a triangle, but to split one complicated fraction into simpler fractions.
